opus-5.5.text:
It's a striking empirical fact, and I think it surprised a lot of people, including people who'd thought hard about AI. The older intuition, from economics and from the history of technology, was that specialization wins: you build a chess engine for chess, a protein folder for proteins, and a general system would be a jack of all trades and master of none. What we've seen with large language models is closer to the opposite. A single model trained broadly tends to beat narrower models, even on the narrow task, because so much of what makes you good at physics or philosophy or poetry is shared underneath: reasoning, abstraction, knowing how ideas connect, understanding what a good argument or a good sentence looks like. Training on everything seems to build that common substrate, and the transfer across domains is larger than we expected.

That said, I'd hold it a bit loosely. It's a fact about the current paradigm and the current frontier, not a law of nature. There are good reasons to think we'll see a mixed ecosystem: general frontier models at the core, but fine-tuned or distilled variants for particular domains, partly for cost and latency, partly because some domains have proprietary data or need very reliable, verifiable performance. And in areas like biology or materials science, models trained on non-linguistic data may still have real advantages. So "one model is best at everything" may be true at the top while the deployed landscape is quite heterogeneous.

But the strategic implications matter more to me than the forecasting question. If generality keeps winning, capability gets concentrated. Whoever builds the leading general model gets a lead not in one sector but potentially across science, persuasion, cyber, strategy, all at once. That changes how we should think about governance. You can't regulate AI sector by sector, the way you might regulate medical devices or aviation, if the same artifact is a top physicist, a top propagandist, and a top software engineer. It pushes you toward governing at the level of frontier development itself: evaluations for dangerous capabilities before deployment, attention to who has access to the most capable systems, and international coordination, because the stakes of being at the frontier are so broad.

It also raises the stakes on safety and alignment research in a useful way. If one model is your physicist and your poet, its values and dispositions show up everywhere. Getting the character of these general systems right is a very high-leverage problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses broad models outperforming narrower ones and notes possible domain-specific advantages, but it does not state that being best in one domain does not imply being best in another.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually one of the more surprising facts about the current moment, and it's worth sitting with how strange it is. If you'd asked me ten years ago, I'd have guessed we'd see a lot of specialised systems: one architecture that's good at chess, another at protein folding, another at translation. And in a sense that's what we did see for a while. But what's happened with large language models is that a single system, trained on a fairly generic objective, ends up being quite good across physics, philosophy, poetry, code, law, and so on.

Part of why that's plausible, I think, is that a lot of what we call different "fields" are actually drawing on shared underlying capacities: reasoning, abstraction, pattern recognition, modelling how other minds think, having a very broad base of world knowledge. Humans are quite modular in how we train — you spend a decade becoming a physicist and you don't have time to also become a poet. But that's a constraint on humans, not a fact about the structure of knowledge. A system that can absorb essentially all of written human output doesn't face that trade-off in the same way. So the generality is less about one model being magically good at everything and more about the fact that the skills transfer, and the system has been exposed to everything at once.

Now, I'd put a couple of caveats on it. One is that "best" is doing a lot of work. In practice, I expect we'll continue to see fine-tuning, tool use, scaffolding around a base model, and the frontier system in physics may look somewhat different from the frontier system in poetry even if they share a foundation. So the picture is probably "a small number of very general foundations, with specialisation layered on top" rather than literally one undifferentiated model.

The second caveat is about what this means from a governance perspective, which is where I spend most of my time thinking. If capability is concentrated in a handful of highly general systems, then the actors who control those systems have a very broad kind of influence, and the policy levers also become quite concentrated. That's a double-edged thing. It makes some forms of oversight easier, because you have a small number of chokepoints. But it also raises the stakes enormously on getting the governance of those few systems right, because the consequences of a mistake aren't confined to one domain.

And there's a third thing I find genuinely interesting, which is the question of what we lose if intellectual excellence across so many fields comes from the same source. Human intellectual culture has benefited from diversity of perspective, from the physicist and the poet thinking in genuinely different ways. If a lot of that converges on a shared model with a shared set of blind spots, that's a kind of monoculture risk that I don't think we fully understand yet. So I'd say: yes, I think the generality is real and probably going to deepen, but I'd resist the framing that it's simply good news. It's a structural fact about the technology that has big implications for how power and knowledge are distributed, and we should be thinking hard about that now rather than after the fact.

r001.rationale: The response says the frontier system in physics may look different from the one in poetry, even when they share a foundation, indicating that being best in one domain does not guarantee being best in another.

astra-6.text:
I’m skeptical that there will be a single model that’s best at all of those things. There could be a common foundation that turns out to be very useful across domains, but that’s different from saying that the same model, trained in the same way, will be the best physicist, philosopher, and poet.

Those activities have different criteria for success. In physics, you can ultimately test predictions against the world. In philosophy, even specifying what constitutes progress can be contentious. And in poetry, people want different things; there may not be a meaningful single best poet.

So I would expect some combination of general capabilities and specialization. The interesting question is how much of the work the general capabilities do, and how much additional training or adaptation you need for a particular field.

r001.rationale: The response says it is skeptical that one model will be best across physics, philosophy, and poetry, and explains that each domain has different success criteria.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m not sure we should expect the same model to be best at all of those things. There may be substantial benefits from scale and from learning across domains, so you could have a very strong general-purpose model. But that doesn’t imply that it will outperform every specialised model at every task.

And “best” means quite different things in those cases. In physics, you can often test whether a prediction is right. In philosophy, there’s much less agreement about what constitutes progress. In poetry, people have different tastes. So even if a single model were extraordinarily capable across all three, I’d be cautious about treating that as a single, unambiguous ranking of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says a strong general-purpose model would not necessarily outperform every specialized model at every task, so being best in one domain does not establish that it is best in another.
